observation.visible_scene: A still-life macro shot against a warm orange-tan gradient background. Several wine corks form a base (one upright cork on the left bears the cursive label 'Barossa'; others lie horizontally). A single translucent/frosted ice shard is balanced on the corks, and a whole green olive rests on the upper-right face of that ice. The camera is fixed; corks and background do not move throughout.
visible_changes: For roughly the first 2.1 seconds (frames 1-33) the scene is static: the olive remains perched in the same position on the ice, with no detectable movement of the olive, ice, or corks.

At about t=2.20 s (frame 34) the olive is no longer intact on the ice; that single frame shows scattered green and pale fragments around the ice face, i.e. an apparent breakup/shatter of the olive (and/or ice) at the moment of transition.

From t=2.27 s to the end (frames 35-41) the olive appears in a new state and location: a flattened, deformed green mass resting low at the base of the ice, in front of the horizontal corks. The ice behind it now shows its frosted top without the olive on it. This deformed mass stays motionless for the remainder of the excerpt.
outside_clip_unknowns: The cause or trigger of the breakup seen between frames 33 and 34 is not shown.
Whether the olive was already moving before the crop boundary, and what happens after the deformed mass settles, are outside the segment.
uncertain_details: It is unclear from the single transitional frame whether the fragments in frame 34 are the olive shattering, the ice cracking, or both.
The exact instant and manner of detachment from the ice (sliding vs. falling vs. bursting) cannot be resolved at this frame rate.
The change from a spherical to a squashed/pear-shaped olive is a real deformation of the object, not occlusion, but the precise impact geometry is not visible.
